title: Caching With Cache Components
summary: Use Cache Components to prerender a static shell, cache data and components with use cache, and expire them by time or by tag.
intro: Trailhead's product list changes a few times a day, but every visit so far has asked the API for it again, and every visitor has waited for the answer. Caching keeps a result and hands it to the next visitor, so the page is ready before anyone asks. Done carelessly, it also shows old prices or one person's cart to another. This lesson covers the layers of caching a request passes through, how Cache Components prerender a static shell, how `use cache` and `cacheLife` keep data, how tags clear it when the data changes, what ISR looks like in Next.js, and how to check what's cached.

steps.title: The layers of caching
steps.body:
Caching isn't one thing in a Next.js app. There are several caches, each in a different place, keeping different things for different lengths of time. When a page shows something old, or asks the API more often than you expect, the first question is which of them is involved.

```diagram cache-components-layers
A visit is answered by the first layer with a fresh copy. Only a miss everywhere reaches the API.
```

## In the browser: the router cache

The router keeps the RSC payloads of pages you've visited or prefetched, in memory, so Back and repeat clicks are instant. Each one stays fresh for its **stale** time, five minutes by default, and the server sends that time with each response, in a header named `x-nextjs-stale-time`. A full reload empties it.

## At the edge: a CDN

Recall CDNs and `Cache-Control` from the web course, and the `s-maxage` and `stale-while-revalidate` you sent by hand in the React course's lesson on rendering on the server: a CDN keeps copies of whole responses on servers near your visitors, for as long as `s-maxage` says, and `stale-while-revalidate` lets it hand out an old copy while it fetches a new one. Next.js writes those headers for you on pages it can cache, from the lifetimes you set in your code. The example below shows them on Trailhead's home page.

## On the server: prerendered pages and the use cache store

The Next.js server keeps two kinds of results that every visitor shares. **Prerendered pages** are the HTML and payload made during the build, or regenerated later, and served without running your components. The **use cache store** holds the results of functions and components you mark with the `use cache` directive, keyed by their arguments, and by default it lives in the server's memory. Both last until they're revalidated, which the rest of this lesson covers.

## Inside one render: React's cache and fetch memoization

The previous lesson's tools work inside a single render. They stop the same request going out twice while one page is made, and forget everything once it's done. They make a page cheaper, but they never make the next visitor's page faster.

## Which one to reach for

Most of your decisions are about the server layer: what to cache, for how long, and how to clear it. The browser's router cache and the CDN follow from those choices, since Next.js sets their times from yours. And the per-render tools are a habit, not a decision: use `cache` for any shared data function that isn't already cached. The rest of this lesson is about the server layer.

examples.title: The headers on a cached page
examples.prompt: With the production server running, look at the caching headers on the home page, which shows three products from `listProducts`, cached for hours.
examples.explanation: `x-nextjs-cache: HIT` says the server answered from a page it had already rendered, without running any components or calling the API. `Cache-Control` is for CDNs and other shared caches. `s-maxage=3600` lets them keep the page for an hour, and `stale-while-revalidate=82800` lets them hand out an older copy for up to 23 hours more while they fetch a fresh one, so the copy is never more than a day old. Those numbers come straight from the `hours` cache profile the page's data uses, which part 3 explains. It's the same pair of headers you wrote by hand for ISR in the React course.

steps.title: Cache Components and the static shell
steps.body:
Every new project has `cacheComponents: true` in `next.config.ts`. That one line changes the question Next.js asks about each page. It no longer asks whether a whole page is static or dynamic. It renders every page during the build as far as it can, and asks you what to do about each part that can't be finished ahead of time.

## Prerendering by default

During `next build`, Next.js renders every route's component tree. Plain components, module imports, reading files in the project, and work that gives the same result every time all finish during the build, and their output is saved. What comes out is the route's **static shell**: HTML, plus the RSC payload for client navigations, that can be served straight away, from the server or a CDN, before any of your code runs for the visitor. Recall partial prerendering from the React course: a static shell with holes that fill in as the request is handled. With Cache Components on, that's simply how every route is built, and it's called **Partial Prerendering**, or PPR.

## Three choices for uncached data

Some work can't finish during the build: a `fetch` or database call whose result isn't cached, `cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`, `params` values nobody listed ahead of time, and `connection()`. When the build meets one, it stops and asks you to choose one of three things:

- **Stream it.** Wrap the part that waits in `<Suspense>`. The fallback goes into the static shell, and the part renders at request time and streams in, as the previous lesson showed.
- **Cache it.** Mark the function or component with `"use cache"`. Its result is computed during the build, joins the static shell, and is kept until it's revalidated. Request data like cookies can't be cached this way, only data that's the same for everyone.
- **Block.** Add `export const instant = false` to the page or layout. Next.js stops checking that the route has a useful shell, and lets it render as a whole on every request, the way server-side rendering worked in the React course. The build lists it as `ƒ`, dynamic.

Stream the parts that differ per request, cache the parts that are the same for everyone, and block only when neither works, say a page that must not show anything until it has checked something on the server.

## Reading the build error

The error is long, but it says the same three things every time: which route, what kind of data it met, and the three fixes, marked `[stream]`, `[cache]`, and `[block]`. The stack under it points at the component it was rendering, which can be a parent of the real culprit. For the exact line, follow its own advice: run `next dev`, open the route, and the terminal and the browser's overlay both point at the `fetch` or the `cookies()` call itself.

The check also runs in development, for every page you open, with the same fixes offered in the overlay. So you can fix each page as you write it, instead of meeting all of them in the build.

examples.title: A page that blocks the build
examples.prompt: `app/products/page.tsx` written the simplest way: it awaits the products at the top, outside any boundary, and `listProducts` isn't cached. Run `npm run build`. The output below starts where the error does.
examples.explanation: The route is `/products`, the data is uncached, and the fixes are the three choices. The stack ends at `CartStoreProvider`, the client provider in the root layout, which is the last component the build had a name for, not the cause. The cause is `await listProducts()` at the top of the page. Wrapping the list in `<Suspense>`, as the previous lesson did, fixes it by streaming. Marking `listProducts` with `"use cache"`, as the next part does, fixes it by caching, and lets the whole list join the static shell.

steps.title: use cache and cacheLife
steps.body:
The product list is the same for every visitor and changes a few times a day. Fetching it on every request wastes the API's time and the visitor's. The `use cache` directive keeps the result and reuses it, and `cacheLife` says for how long.

## The directive

`"use cache"` is a directive like `"use client"`, a string at the top of a body. Put it in three places:

- **At the top of an async function**, to cache what it returns. This is the usual place: the data functions in `lib/products.ts`.
- **At the top of a component**, to cache its rendered output, JSX and all.
- **At the top of a file**, to cache every function the file exports.

The first call runs the function and stores its result. Later calls with the same arguments get the stored result, within one render and across requests, until it expires. During the build, a cached function runs once and its result becomes part of the static shell.

## Arguments are the key

A cached result is stored under a **cache key** made from the function's identity and its arguments, serialized. So `getProduct("ember-stove")` and `getProduct("ridge-2p-tent")` get separate entries, and `listProducts("tents")` doesn't collide with `listProducts()`. Values the function uses from outside, like a variable from an enclosing function, are captured and become part of the key too. That's why arguments must be serializable, like props crossing to a client component: strings and numbers, plain objects, and arrays, not class instances or functions. Pass the plain slug, not a whole request object.

## cacheLife and its profiles

`cacheLife`, imported from `next/cache`, sets how long the entry lives, and the docs recommend calling it in every cached function. It takes three times:

- **stale**: how long the browser's router may reuse it without asking the server.
- **revalidate**: after this, the next request still gets the cached result, and a fresh one is made in the background. That's stale-while-revalidate.
- **expire**: after this long with no requests, the entry is gone, and the next request waits for a fresh one.

Name a profile instead of writing the numbers:

| Profile | stale | revalidate | expire |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `default` | 5 minutes | 15 minutes | never |
| `seconds` | 30 seconds | 1 second | 1 minute |
| `minutes` | 5 minutes | 1 minute | 1 hour |
| `hours` | 5 minutes | 1 hour | 1 day |
| `days` | 5 minutes | 1 day | 1 week |
| `weeks` | 5 minutes | 1 week | 30 days |
| `max` | 5 minutes | 30 days | 1 year |

Pick by how stale the data may be, not by how often it changes. A product's name and price can be an hour old, so `hours`. Reviews should show up within a minute or so, so `minutes`. You can define your own profiles in `next.config.ts` under `cacheLife`. A very short life, like `seconds`, can't be part of the static shell, since it would be out of date before anyone saw it, so its part streams in at request time instead.

When cached functions call each other, the outer entry can't outlive the inner ones: a page that uses both `hours` and `minutes` data revalidates every minute.

## No request data inside

A cached result is shared by everyone, so it must not depend on who's asking. That's why `cookies()`, `headers()`, and `searchParams` are refused inside `use cache`, even when a helper deep inside calls them. Read them outside, in an uncached component, and pass the value you need as an argument, so it becomes part of the key. Then only requests with the same value share an entry.

examples.title: Cached data functions
examples.prompt: The data functions in `lib/products.ts`, now cached. The schemas and imports above them are as before, plus `import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from "next/cache";`.
examples.explanation: Each cached function starts with the directive, then sets its life and its tag, which the next part uses. `getProduct` no longer needs React's `cache`, since `use cache` already reuses results within a render. The `try` and `catch` sit inside the cached function on purpose: a missing product is cached as `null`, a normal result. An error thrown out of a cached function reaches the caller without its class or message in production, so an `instanceof ApiError` check outside would fail and turn a 404 into a crash. `getStock` is left uncached, since stock changes by the minute, and the rendering lesson streams it as a hole in the product page.

examples.title: A cookie inside use cache
examples.prompt: `app/lab/page.tsx` has a cached function that calls `apiFetch("/cart", { session: true })`, which reads the session cookie, and its page awaits it. Build the project. The output below starts where the error does.
examples.explanation: The error names `cookies()`, says it can't be read inside `"use cache"`, and gives the fix. The stack shows the chain: the cached `getCart` in the page called `apiFetch`, and `apiFetch` read the cookie at line 15, so the rule follows the call into the helper. A cart belongs to one person, so it shouldn't be in a shared cache at all: read it uncached, inside `Suspense`. If you really need to cache per-user data, read the cookie outside and pass the user's id as an argument, so each user gets their own entry, or use the `use cache: private` variant from the last part of this lesson.

steps.title: Tags and revalidation
steps.body:
A cache that only expires on a timer shows old data until the timer runs out. When you know the data changed, because your own app just changed it or the API told you so, you want to clear exactly the entries that hold it, and nothing else. Tags are how you name those entries.

## cacheTag

`cacheTag("products")`, called inside a cached function, attaches a tag to its entry. One entry can have several tags, and one tag can be on many entries. Trailhead tags by what the data is about: `products` for the list, `product-ember-stove` for one product, `reviews-ember-stove` for its reviews. Name tags after the data, not the page, since the same data shows up on several pages.

## updateTag, after your own writes

When a Server Action, the function a form calls on the server, changes data, call `updateTag` with the tag of what changed. It expires those entries at once, so the very next render waits for fresh data. That's **read-your-own-writes**: someone posts a review, and the page they're taken back to shows it. `updateTag` works only inside Server Actions, which the next section of the course covers in full.

```diagram cache-components-tags
The read stores an entry under a tag, the write expires every entry with that tag, and the next read makes a fresh one.
```

In step 1, `getProduct("ember-stove")` runs and stores the product under `product-ember-stove`. In step 2, an action saves a new price to the API and calls `updateTag("product-ember-stove")`. In step 3, the next render finds the entry expired, runs `getProduct` again, and stores the new price. Every page that shows the Ember Stove's price gets the new one, because they all read the same entry.

## revalidateTag, for changes from elsewhere

Sometimes the change happens outside your app: someone edits a price in the warehouse system, and it calls a URL on your site to say so. That's a **webhook**, a request one system sends another when something happens. Handle it in a Route Handler, a file that answers HTTP requests, and call `revalidateTag(tag, "max")`. Unlike `updateTag`, it doesn't make anyone wait: the next request still gets the old entry, and a fresh one is made in the background. The second argument is how long old content may still be served while that happens, and `"max"` means the old copy is always good enough to show once more. Use `updateTag` when the person who made the change is about to look, and `revalidateTag` with `"max"` when nobody is waiting.

## revalidatePath and refresh

`revalidatePath("/products")` expires everything on one page, whatever tags its data has. It's a blunt tool, handy when you don't know the tags, but tags are more precise. And `refresh()`, also from `next/cache`, tells the browser's router to fetch the current page again after a Server Action, without expiring anything on the server, for data that was never cached, like the cart.

examples.title: Expiring a tag after a write
examples.prompt: The shape of a Server Action that posts a review and then expires the product's reviews. The Server Actions lesson builds it in full, with validation and errors.
examples.explanation: `"use server"` at the top makes every export in the file a Server Function, which a form can call. After the API has saved the review, `updateTag` expires every entry tagged `reviews-ember-stove`, or whichever product it was. When the action finishes, Next.js renders the page again for the person who posted, and `getReviews` finds its entry expired, so it asks the API and gets the new review. The product's name and price are tagged differently, so they stay cached. Forgetting the `updateTag` is the classic bug: the review is saved, and the page doesn't show it for up to a minute.

examples.title: A webhook that revalidates a tag
examples.prompt: `app/api/revalidate/route.ts` lets another system clear a tag. `REVALIDATE_SECRET` is set in `.env.local`, so only callers who know it are accepted.
examples.explanation: A `route.ts` file answers HTTP requests at its folder's URL, here `/api/revalidate`, and exporting `POST` handles POST requests. The Route Handlers lesson covers them properly. The secret check matters: without it, anyone could clear your caches over and over and make every page slow. `revalidateTag(tag, "max")` marks the entries stale. It doesn't render anything itself: the next visitor to each affected page still gets the old version, and that visit starts the regeneration. The next part runs it and watches the page change.

steps.title: ISR the Next.js way
steps.body:
Incremental Static Regeneration, ISR from the React course, is static pages that renew themselves: served as fast as static files, regenerated after a while or when told. In the React course you built it from HTTP headers and a CDN. In Next.js it's what you get from `use cache` with a lifetime, plus a list of pages to build ahead of time.

## Time-based

A page whose data is all cached gets the shortest lifetime of that data. When a request arrives after the `revalidate` time, the server hands out the page it has and renders a fresh one in the background, and the request after that gets the new one. After `expire` with no visits at all, the next visitor waits for a fresh render. On the wire, it becomes the headers you wrote by hand in the React course: `s-maxage` from `revalidate`, and `stale-while-revalidate` for the rest of the time until `expire`. The `hours` profile gave Trailhead's home page `s-maxage=3600, stale-while-revalidate=82800`.

## On demand

When the data changes before the timer runs out, `revalidateTag` from a webhook, or `updateTag` from an action, marks the page's data stale, and the next visit starts a fresh render. The example below does exactly that with the webhook from the previous part.

## Pages listed ahead of time

A route with a dynamic segment, like `app/products/[slug]`, has a page for every product, and the build doesn't know the slugs on its own. Export `generateStaticParams` from the page, returning the values to build, and each one is prerendered like a static page:

```tsx sketch
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const products = await listProducts();
  return products.map((product) => ({ slug: product.slug }));
}
```

It can call cached functions, so the list itself comes from the cache. A slug that wasn't on the list, like a product added after the build, still works. Its first visitor gets the route's App Shell, the shared shell from the routing lesson, with the product's parts streaming in, and in the background Next.js renders the complete page for that slug and keeps it. The next visitor gets it as a static page. Trailhead's help pages behave this way: `/help/warranty`, which isn't on their list, came back private and streamed on the first request, and as a cache `HIT` on the second.

## Reading it in the route table

With lifetimes in play, the build's route table grows two columns, **Revalidate** and **Expire**, for each prerendered page. The rendering lesson reads the table in full. The example below shows the lines for the home page and the product pages.

examples.title: The route table with lifetimes
examples.prompt: After caching the data functions and adding `generateStaticParams` to the product page, build again, printing from the route table on.
examples.explanation: The home page is `○` with `1h` and `1d`, the `hours` profile of `listProducts`. Each product page is listed by its slug, since `generateStaticParams` named them, and the table shows two and counts the rest. Their lifetime is `1m` and `1h`: the page uses `getProduct` with `hours`, and `getReviews` with `minutes`, and the shorter one wins. They're `◐`, not `○`, because the stock is an uncached hole that streams at request time. `/products/[slug]` on its own line is the App Shell for slugs not on the list. `/api/revalidate` is `ƒ`, since a POST handler always runs on demand.

examples.title: Revalidating on demand
examples.prompt: After the build, Sam bought the last nine Summit Daypack 22L packs, so the API now says the pack is out of stock. With the production server running, save this as `isr.sh` and run it with `bash isr.sh`.

check() { curl -s -D headers.txt -o page.html http://127.0.0.1:3005/ grep -i x-nextjs-cache headers.txt grep -o -E 'Summit Daypack 22L

[^<]*

(

[^<]*

The second check is `STALE`: the server sent the old page one last time and started rendering a new one in the background, which is stale-while-revalidate. A second later, the third check is a `HIT` with Out of stock under the price. No build, no deploy, and only the pages that use the `products` tag were touched.

steps.title: Seeing what is cached
steps.body:
Caching bugs are quiet. Nothing crashes: a page shows an old price, or asks the API on every visit when it shouldn't, or, worst, shows one person's data to another. So check what's cached as you build, instead of waiting for a customer to notice.

## The route table and the response headers

The build's route table is the overview: `○` for a page that's entirely prerendered, `◐` for a shell with holes, `ƒ` for a page rendered on every request, and the Revalidate and Expire columns for how long each lasts. When a page you expected to be `○` comes out `◐`, something in it reads request data or uncached data, so look for the hole.

On a running production server, the `x-nextjs-cache` response header says what happened to one request: `HIT` for a stored page, `STALE` for an old one served while a fresh one is made, `MISS` when it had to render. `x-nextjs-postponed: 1` means the response had holes that streamed.

## The dev log

With `logging.fetches` turned on in `next.config.ts`, the dev server lists every fetch under each page request. A fetch inside a cached function shows up the first time, and then not again until the entry expires. So a second visit with no fetch lines under it means the cache answered. The example below shows it. For more detail, start the server with `NEXT_PRIVATE_DEBUG_CACHE=1` in front of the command, and it logs every cache read and write. In development, a `console.log` inside a cached function is replayed with a `Cache` label, so you can tell it apart from code that really ran.

## Mistakes to watch for

- **Caching per-user data.** A cart, an account page, anything that depends on the cookie. The cache key is only the arguments, so a cached function without the user in its arguments would hand one user's data to everyone. Next.js refuses `cookies()` inside `use cache` for this reason, but you can still get it wrong by passing data in some other way. Keep personal data uncached, inside `Suspense`.
- **Missing tags.** An entry with no tag can only expire on its timer. Tag every cached function by the data it holds, so a write can clear it.
- **The current time in cached code.** `Date.now()` or `new Date()` inside a cached function runs once, and the time is frozen into the entry. A line like Updated 2 minutes ago would say the same thing for an hour. Compute times outside, in an uncached component with `connection()`, or in the browser.
- **Throwing for expected results.** Return `null` or an empty list for a missing product or no reviews, as `getProduct` does, rather than throwing out of a cached function.

## The other two cache directives

Two variants of the directive exist for special cases, and you'll see them in the docs:

- `"use cache: private"` may read `cookies()` and `headers()`. Its results are kept only for one request on the server, and in the visitor's own browser for the stale time, never in a shared cache. It's for personal data that's slow to compute and worth reusing across one person's navigations.
- `"use cache: remote"` stores results in a shared cache outside the server's memory, like Redis, a fast store that keeps its data in memory on a server of its own, through a cache handler your host provides. Plain `use cache` keeps entries in each server's memory, so with several servers, or a host that starts a fresh one per request, entries are lost often. Remote fixes that, at the cost of a network trip per lookup.

Both shipped with Cache Components in Next.js 16.0. Start with plain `use cache`, and reach for these only when you measure a need.

examples.title: Two visits in the dev log
examples.prompt: The dev server's log for two visits to the home page, then two to the Ember Stove's page, with `logging.fetches` on.
examples.explanation: The first visit to `/` fetched the product list, 313 milliseconds, and took 598 in all. The second took 26 milliseconds with no fetch at all: `listProducts` answered from the `use cache` store. On the product page, the first visit fetched the product twice and the reviews once. One product fetch was `getProduct`, cached, and the other was `getStock`, which isn't. The second visit made only the stock fetch, and took 250 milliseconds instead of 1,734. The `(cache skip)` on each line is about Next.js's separate fetch cache, which `use cache` replaces, so it doesn't mean the result wasn't kept. You now have every piece that decides how a page is made: request data, streaming, and caching. The next lesson puts them together, page by page, as rendering modes.

recap:
- A request can be answered by the browser's router cache, a CDN, the server's prerendered pages and use cache store, or the per-render tools, before it reaches the API.
- With cacheComponents on, every route is prerendered as far as possible into a static shell.
- Uncached data has three answers: stream it in Suspense, cache it with use cache, or block with export const instant = false.
- use cache keys entries by the function and its serializable arguments, and cacheLife sets stale, revalidate, and expire.
- Request data like cookies() can't be read inside use cache. Read it outside and pass a value in.
- cacheTag names entries, updateTag expires them after your own writes, and revalidateTag(tag, "max") refreshes them in the background.
- ISR in Next.js is cached data with a lifetime, generateStaticParams for pages built ahead, and on-demand revalidation.
- Check caching with the route table, x-nextjs-cache, and the dev log, and never cache per-user data.
